items.title: How the CMB was found
items.claim: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered the cosmic microwave background in 1964 while working at Bell Labs. What were they originally trying to do?

options.text: Refining a horn antenna for radio communications, with the persistent noise traced to a cosmic source

items.reveal_title: An accidental discovery in a communications lab
items.reveal:
Penzias and Wilson were eliminating noise sources, including pigeon droppings inside the antenna. The Princeton group nearby was independently looking for exactly this signal.

Nobel Prize 1978 went to Penzias and Wilson.
items.why: Major cosmological evidence has come from accident as often as from targeted experiment.

items.title: First imaged black hole
items.claim: The Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of a supermassive black hole in 2019. Which one?

options.text: Sagittarius A* in the Milky Way
The black hole at the centre of M87, around 53 million light-years away
A solar-mass black hole in Cygnus

items.reveal_title: M87* came first; Sagittarius A* followed in 2022
items.reveal:
EHT's M87* image released 10 April 2019; Sagittarius A* image released 12 May 2022. M87* is roughly 6.5 billion solar masses; Sagittarius A* is around 4 million.

EHT combines radio telescopes on multiple continents to create an Earth-sized aperture.
items.why: Imaging the largest objects in the universe required a planet-sized synthetic instrument.

items.title: Lunar samples returned
items.claim: How much lunar material did the six Apollo missions return to Earth in total?
items.reveal:
Apollo 11 returned about 22 kg; later missions returned larger samples. Soviet Luna robotic missions returned around 0.3 kg.

China's Chang'e 5 (2020) returned around 1.7 kg.
items.why: Sample-return missions remain extremely costly per gram delivered, shaping research priorities.
